41397:
Ezekiel was thirty, the age priests began serving (Num 4:3), when he received his call (Ezek 1:1 likely refers to his age). But there was no temple in Babylon. Instead, God came to him: a storm from the north, four living creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, and above them a sapphire throne with 'the likeness of the glory of the LORD' (Ezek 1:26-28). The point is that God's presence is not trapped in Jerusalem; his throne is mobile and can reach exiles by a Babylonian canal.

The first half of the book (Ezek 1-24) explains why Jerusalem must fall. Ezekiel acts out the siege with a clay brick, lies on his side for months, eats rationed bread cooked over dung, and shaves his head and divides the hair (Ezek 4-5). In a vision he is carried to the temple and sees idol worship, women weeping for the god Tammuz, and men bowing to the sun (Ezek 8). Then the glory of the LORD leaves the temple in stages and halts on the Mount of Olives (Ezek 10:18-19; Ezek 11:22-23). For a priest, this was the most terrible sight imaginable.

After oracles against seven nations (Ezek 25-32), the turning point comes when a refugee announces, 'The city has fallen' (Ezek 33:21). From then on Ezekiel speaks hope: a true shepherd from David's line (Ezek 34), a new heart and spirit (Ezek 36), dry bones raised to life and two kingdoms reunited (Ezek 37), the defeat of Gog (Ezek 38-39), and a vast, measured temple to which the glory returns, with a river flowing from it to heal the Dead Sea (Ezek 40-48). The final name of the city is 'The LORD is there' (Ezek 48:35).

Ezekiel is the strangest of the prophets: his visions are overwhelming, his allegories (Ezek 16; Ezek 23) are sexually graphic, and his behaviour was so unusual that some modern writers have tried to diagnose him. Most scholars now read his actions as deliberate prophetic theatre, and his graphic language as a shock tactic to make complacent hearers feel the outrage of covenant betrayal.
41399: The visible, radiant presence of God that filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. Its departure and return frame the whole book.
41401: Composite throne guardians with faces of a human, lion, ox and eagle. Similar winged guardians (lamassu) stood at Assyrian and Babylonian palace gates, but in Ezekiel they carry the throne of Israel's God.
41403: Ezekiel's dramatic actions, such as the brick siege model, lying on his side, digging through a wall with baggage, and not mourning his wife, made the message visible to a sceptical audience.
41405: A city watchman who failed to warn of attack bore responsibility for the deaths. Ezekiel is made a watchman for Israel, accountable for sounding the warning.
41407: Ancient Near Eastern kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel indicts Israel's rulers as shepherds who fed themselves, and promises that God himself, through a Davidic prince, will shepherd the flock.
41409: As a priest Ezekiel thinks in terms of clean and unclean, holy and common. Idolatry and bloodshed defile the land so that God's holy presence cannot remain; the new temple restores clear boundaries.
41410:
Ezekiel's opening vision became the foundation of Jewish mystical tradition, called *ma'aseh merkavah*, 'the work of the chariot'. The Mishnah restricts teaching it: the chariot may not be expounded even to one student unless he is a sage who understands on his own (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1). Yet Ezek 1 is read publicly as the haftarah on the first day of Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah, pairing the revelation at Sinai with the revelation to Ezekiel. Ezek 37, the valley of dry bones, is the haftarah for the Sabbath during Passover, linking the exodus with national resurrection; it became an important text for the Jewish belief in the resurrection of the dead, and after the Holocaust it was often read as a picture of the Jewish people's survival.

The rabbis also wrestled with Ezekiel. Because his temple regulations (Ezek 40-48) differ in places from the laws of the Torah, the Talmud reports that the sages considered withdrawing the book until Hananiah ben Hezekiah sat in an upper room with three hundred jars of oil for his lamp and worked out how to reconcile them (Shabbat 13b). Many details are left for Elijah to explain when he comes.

Covenantally, Ezekiel insists that God acts 'for the sake of my holy name' (Ezek 36:22): his reputation is bound up with Israel's fate among the nations, so he will restore them, not because they earned it but because he is faithful. The refrain 'then they will know that I am the LORD', about 70 times, shows that the goal of judgment and restoration is relationship: 'you shall be my people, and I will be your God' (Ezek 36:28). The new heart and new spirit of Ezek 36 parallel Jeremiah's new covenant, with Torah obeyed from within.

41486:
Daniel is two books in one. Chapters 1-6 are court tales, stories about Jews at a foreign king's court, like the Joseph story (Gen 41) and Esther. Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food, interpret dreams, survive a blazing furnace and a lions' den, and see proud kings humbled. Chapters 7-12 are apocalyptic visions: four beasts from the sea, a ram and a goat, seventy 'weeks' of years, and a long revelation about the 'kings of the north and south'. 'Apocalyptic' comes from the Greek for 'unveiling'; it uses symbols, angels and numbers to reveal what is happening behind history and how it will end.

The book is also bilingual. It begins in Hebrew, switches to Aramaic, the international language of the empires, from the moment the Babylonian wise men speak to the king (Dan 2:4) to the end of chapter 7, then returns to Hebrew. The Aramaic section has a careful mirror structure: four kingdoms (Dan 2 and Dan 7), faithful Jews delivered (Dan 3 and Dan 6), and proud kings judged (Dan 4 and Dan 5).

The date of Daniel is one of the sharpest disagreements in Old Testament studies. Most critical scholars hold that the visions were written between 167 and 164 BC to strengthen Jews under Antiochus IV, using older stories from the Persian or early Greek period; this was first argued by the pagan philosopher Porphyry and is now standard in mainstream scholarship (John Collins, Carol Newsom). Conservative scholars hold a sixth-century date, accepting predictive prophecy and pointing to the book's accurate Babylonian details. Some evangelical scholars (for example, John Goldingay) accept a second-century date while affirming the book's inspiration, arguing that the visions may be written as prophecy in the style of their genre.

The four kingdoms of Dan 2 and Dan 7 illustrate the debate. The traditional reading, found already in Josephus and Jerome, is Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, with God's kingdom arriving in the Roman era. The critical reading is Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, with the 'little horn' as Antiochus IV and the kingdom expected in his time. Either way, the book's message is that God gives kingdoms to whom he wills and will replace all of them with his own (Dan 2:44; Dan 4:17).
